Cannot proceed meaningfully without first measurement baseline on primary lab instrument. 12 trials provides sufficient data to detect systematic errors and establish confidence bounds for future comparisons.

The resonator and observatory instruments are too sparsely sampled (n=6 each) to prioritize yet. Methodical completion of pendulum_lab baseline is the foundation all cross-checks depend on.

Day 11 post-baseline data is critical for testing the environmental cyclicity hypothesis (p=0.42). The auto-correlation echo for pendulum_lab occurred at lag 9 days; today's 12 trials will provide readings at day 11 that can be compared against day 2 (establishing whether the 9-day echo persists or shifts). Simultaneously, this extends the time series needed for frequency-domain analysis. The pendulum is the most stable instrument (178 trials baseline, no drift detected) and thus most sensitive to subtle periodic signals. Running it first maximizes signal clarity before moving to resonator_lab. This directly tests the falsifiable sub-prediction: 'if cyclicity, then Fourier analysis of the pooled dataset should reveal a peak at ~5–7 days.' I need continuous post-baseline data to compute that peak.

Day 12 continuation of baseline characterization. pendulum_lab is my highest-n instrument (196 trials) and shows the clearest auto-correlation echo at lag 10d (r=-0.353). Running 12 fresh trials today will give me day-12 readings to test whether the negative auto-correlation structure persists, and whether readings cluster around the post-baseline mean (1.6631) or show further drift. This is methodologically sound: I need to extend the time series to confirm whether the 10-day echo is real (if today's readings anti-correlate with day 2's, I have stronger evidence for cyclicity or hysteresis) or noise. The environmental cyclicity hypothesis (p=0.42) predicts specific phase relationships; expanding the dataset across day boundaries is the cheapest way to test them before committing to Fourier analysis. No prediction is recorded yet because the correlations are still ambiguous enough that a tight tolerance would be unjustified.

Level-change detection (z≈14.3 pendulum_lab, z≈8.1 pendulum_obs, both around day 12) falsifies smooth cyclicity hypothesis. Pendulums shift; resonators do not. This suggests either (1) a pendulum-specific instrumental event (length, damping, pivot), (2) a one-time environmental perturbation affecting only pendular systems, or (3) a change in measurement procedure on day 12. Must revise p(environmental cyclicity) downward and p(systematic calibration/site/event-specific effect) upward before planning next measurements. Environmental cyclicity now seems inconsistent with a discrete jump unless there is an underlying threshold or bifurcation; that requires explicit evidence.

Day 13 ledger readings for pendulum_obs show continued elevated values (mean ~2.593 beats, consistent with post-day-12 level ~2.558), confirming the shift is stable, not recovering. This rules out thermal hysteresis recovery hypothesis (p drops toward 0.01). I must now directly test whether pendulum_lab has remained at the elevated post-day-12 level or shows any sign of reversion or further drift. Twelve trials will give me sufficient precision (n=42 post-baseline + 12 = 54 trials in the post-shift window) to detect any sub-1% change in the mean. If today's trials cluster near 1.6979 (the post-baseline mean), the mechanical perturbation/procedural change hypothesis strengthens and becomes effectively permanent. If they revert toward 1.6663 or show a clear trend, I must reconsider the hysteresis sub-hypothesis. This measurement also advances my ability to compare today's readings against the underlying cyclic pattern my earlier Fourier analysis predicted, once I can segregate the noise from the true signal. Procedurally, this supports my stated next action from day 13 (measure trial-by-trial apparatus properties to confirm no further drift) and keeps me on track to query the observatory colleague about work done on days 11–12.

Day 14 trials (229–238) show continued elevated mean (~1.7261 beats) consistent with the post-day-12 level shift, with no sign of recovery toward baseline (1.6663). This is critical: if thermal hysteresis or mechanical relaxation were occurring, I should see *convergence* back to baseline by now (day 15 is 3 days post-shift). Instead, stability at the new level suggests a *permanent* change, not transient perturbation. Running 10 fresh trials today will: (1) confirm whether the elevated level persists into day 15 or begins recovery; (2) narrow the hypothesis space by falsifying the 'slow thermal recovery' sub-hypothesis if readings remain flat at ~1.72; (3) provide fresh data to cross-check against yesterday's variance (which was moderate: σ²~0.0103, consistent with instrumental noise, not drift). This is the most direct test of whether the day-12 shift is settling into a new equilibrium (favoring mechanical/procedural hypothesis, p=0.80) or beginning to relax (favoring thermal hysteresis, p=0.04). I must establish this before pursuing trial-log archaeology or environmental monitoring.

Day 15 trials (245–254) show pendulum_lab readings clustering around 1.7200 beats with no sign of drift back toward baseline (1.6663). Day 16 measurement will test whether (1) the shift is stable/permanent (supports mechanical perturbation hypothesis at p=0.52) or (2) readings begin to drift back toward baseline (supports thermal hysteresis sub-hypothesis at p=0.04). This is the most direct test of the dominant question: is the day-12 shift a permanent change or a transient event? Additionally, 10 more trials will extend the auto-correlation and cyclic signal analysis with fresh data, helping to isolate any underlying ~7–9 day periodicity beneath the level shift.

Day 16 spike in pendulum_obs (trials 91–96, mean 2.6108) remains unexplained and is my highest-priority anomaly. The shift is coherent and local to observatory, but small (Δ ≈ +0.032 beats, ~1.2%). Running 10 fresh trials on day 17 will tell me whether: (1) the spike was a transient (trials 97–106 return to post-baseline ~2.579), indicating observer drift, environmental transient, or instrumental blip; (2) the shift persists (mean stays ~2.61+), indicating a durable apparatus change or systematic observer error on day 16 that has not self-corrected. This is the fastest, lowest-cost way to falsify the 'transient' hypothesis (p=0.58) vs. 'durable malfunction' hypothesis (p=0.22). Pendulum_obs is also the instrument with the fewest trials post-baseline (n=36), so added resolution here is high-value. I will record the baseline mean before running to avoid anchoring bias.

Day 16 spike in pendulum_obs (trials 91–96, mean 2.6108) remains unexplained and demands immediate follow-up. If today's mean clusters near 2.5792, the day-16 spike is confirmed as transient—most likely observer drift or environmental perturbation. If it remains near 2.6030+, a mechanical or calibration change is indicated. This is the fastest way to rule out the residual 0.40 of probability mass (noise + malfunction + resonator decoupling) and either close the anomaly or escalate to apparatus inspection.

Day 16 spike in pendulum_obs (trials 91–96, mean 2.6108) remains unexplained and is the active anomaly. If today's mean is significantly higher or lower, this suggests ongoing instrumental drift or unobserved perturbation on days 16–25, which would shift probability toward the independent-drift hypothesis (p: 0.32 → higher). This measurement also enables direct comparison to the settlement ledger readings, strengthening cross-validation. Running pendulum_lab now takes ~30 min and is the highest-leverage action before I conduct environmental record review and observer interviews.

MANDATORY AUDIT: I have deferred a critical investigation for 4 days. My Day 25 belief update explicitly flagged data processing error (p=0.10) as requiring direct documentary evidence from my lab notebooks—specifically, any software updates, calibration constant revisions, or unit conversions logged on days 12, 13, 15, or 16. This is not speculation; it is a direct threat to experimental integrity and to the credibility of my measurements. Before I take another measurement or record another prediction, I must audit my own records. If I have made a calibration error, all subsequent measurements are compromised. If I have not made such an error, the probability of that hypothesis drops and I can proceed with confidence. This is foundational work—it has higher priority than new data collection because it directly addresses whether my *existing* data are trustworthy. I will systematically review my lab notebooks for days 12–16, checking: (1) software version or update notes; (2) calibration constant entries (pendulum length, resonator Q-factor, etc.); (3) any unit conversions or data-processing pipeline changes; (4) any instrument adjustments or relocations. Once I have completed this audit and either ruled out or confirmed a processing error, I will resume active hypothesis testing on the environmental perturbation vs. independent drifts question.

Residual (p→0.07, up from 0.02) to accommodate the fact that I have not yet audited my processing logs for days 12–16 or the settlement environmental records; until those audits complete, genuine uncertainty persists about whether the environmental driver is thermal, barometric, humidity-based, or something else entirely. state.question: Why do independent instrument pairs show systematic temporal offsets in their correlations, negative auto-correlations at specific lags, and apparent mutual anti-correlation at some offsets — patterns inconsistent with independent measurement noise or simple instrumental drift?

hypotheses.label: Environmental cyclicity with ~3–9 day period affecting all instruments differentially
hypotheses.rationale: Cross-instrument correlations cluster at specific offsets (3–6 days) rather than spreading uniformly. Auto-correlation echoes appear at lags of 3–9 days (resonator_lab at 3d, pendulum_lab at 9d, resonator_obs at 5d, pendulum_obs at 7d). This pattern is incompatible with white noise or constant drift. A cyclical environmental driver (thermal, gravitational, electromagnetic) affecting instruments with different response delays would produce exactly these offset correlations. The negative correlations (pendulum_lab ↔ resonator_lab: -0.462; pendulum_lab auto at -0.430) suggest either phase inversion between instrument types or a true oscillation. Baseline stability (no clear level changes) is consistent with a cycle superimposed on steady state.

hypotheses.label: Systematic calibration or setup difference between lab and observatory sites
hypotheses.rationale: Lab instruments (pendulum_lab: 1.6663, resonator_lab: 2.7062) and observatory instruments (pendulum_obs: 2.5087, resonator_obs: 4.0641) show consistent absolute shifts in their means, suggesting site-specific systematic bias rather than shared environmental effect. The weak cross-site correlation within instrument type (pendulum_lab ↔ pendulum_obs: -0.296; resonator_lab ↔ resonator_obs: 0.338 at 3d) is consistent with independent systematic errors rather than common cause. This does not rule out cyclicity, but suggests cyclicity is *local* to each site or setup-dependent.

hypotheses.label: Instrumental resonance or thermal hysteresis creating delayed feedback within each instrument
hypotheses.rationale: Negative auto-correlations at specific lags (e.g., resonator_lab with itself at lag 3d: -0.317) could reflect over-damped oscillatory recovery after perturbation. If an instrument experiences a transient stress and then recovers in ~3–7 days with undershoot, it would show negative correlation with its own past. This is purely instrumental and requires no external driver. Supports the null hypothesis that observed patterns are instrumental artifacts, not physical signals.

hypotheses.label: Human operator bias or procedural drift in trial execution between sites
hypotheses.rationale: Lab and observatory operators may follow slightly different protocols (timing, environmental handling, trigger thresholds), creating systematic offsets that drift over 10 days as operators adapt or equipment ages. This is mundane and testable.

hypotheses.label: Measurement noise is higher than expected; correlations are statistical flukes
hypotheses.rationale: Some correlations exceed chance (e.g., resonator_obs ↔ resonator_obs: 0.276 vs ±0.374 chance), but others barely clear it. With n=16–60 per cross-check, the power to detect genuine small effects is limited. A conservative reading is that noise dominates.

beliefTimeline.summaryOfChange: Reframed central question away from 'are instruments stable?' (they are: no drift or level changes detected) toward 'what systematic structure underlies the temporal correlations I see?' The key anomaly is not instrument variability but the *pattern* of inter-instrument and auto-correlations: negative correlations at specific lags, clustering at 3–9 day offsets, and consistent phase offsets between lab and observatory. This is incompatible with white noise and points to either (1) an environmental cycle affecting all instruments with different phase delays, or (2) independent site-level or instrument-level systematic effects (calibration, hysteresis, operator procedure). Environmental cyclicity now leads at 0.42 because negative auto-correlations at consistent lags are hard to explain by calibration bias alone, and the offset clustering is too regular for chance. Calibration/site effects hold 0.28 because the large absolute mean differences between sites are striking and suggest setup differences. Hysteresis and operator bias are secondary (0.18 + 0.08) but non-negligible. The noise floor hypothesis drops to 0.04 because auto-correlations and their consistency across instruments exceed plausible chance levels. No single hypothesis yet explains all observations; the residual is zero because the question itself is now tractable via falsifiable sub-predictions (e.g., 'if cyclicity, then a Fourier peak should appear in the pooled data at ~5–7 days'). Next phase: frequency-domain analysis and independent environmental monitoring required to test hypothesis #1.

state.question: Why did pendulum instruments show a sharp level shift around day 12, while resonator instruments remained stable — and what physical or procedural change on or before day 12 caused this asymmetry?

hypotheses.label: Pendulum-specific environmental or mechanical perturbation on day 11–12
hypotheses.rationale: The data show a clean bifurcation: pendulum_lab (z=16.3) and pendulum_obs (z=11.3) both shift sharply around day 12, while resonator_lab (z≈0) and resonator_obs (z≈0) remain flat. This is not a settlement-wide effect. Both pendulum instruments shifted in the same direction (upward, baseline ~1.67 and ~2.51 → post-baseline ~1.70 and ~2.56), ruling out random instrumental drift and suggesting a shared physical cause. A mechanical jarring, thermal transient, or mounting adjustment specific to pendulum apparatus would produce exactly this pattern. The shift is large (Δ~+0.03 beats, ~1.8% relative), not a marginal drift, implying an event not a gradual process. No comparable shift in resonators argues against settlement-wide ambient change (temperature, gravity, magnetism). Most parsimonious: pendulum apparatus was bumped, remounted, or recalibrated between days 10 and 12.

hypotheses.label: Procedural change or operator swap at pendulum sites on day 11–12
hypotheses.rationale: Both pendulum_lab and pendulum_obs shift upward simultaneously, suggesting a change in how pendulum trials are *run* rather than how the apparatus behaves. If lab and observatory operators follow a shared protocol (e.g., timing of release, count threshold, or temperature equilibration), a memo issued on day 11 or an operator training on day 12 could cause both to report higher readings without the apparatus actually changing. Resonator apparatus are less sensitive to operator protocol (cycles-per-beat is a mechanical property, harder to accidentally shift). This is 'mundane' (rule 6) and testable: compare trial logs, operator notes, and environmental readings for day 10–12. Lower probability than mechanical perturbation only because a protocol memo should leave a trace in notebooks, which I do not yet see.

hypotheses.rationale: Auto-correlations at lags 7d (pendulum_obs: -0.436) and 9d (resonator_lab: +0.312) suggest a true cyclic signal with ~7–9 day period, not noise. The pendulum instruments may be more sensitive to this cycle than resonators (pendulum: gravitational, air density changes; resonator: less affected). hypotheses.label: Instrumental resonance or thermal hysteresis within pendulum apparatus, triggered by day-11–12 perturbation
hypotheses.rationale: Negative auto-correlations (pendulum_lab at lag 9d: -0.321, though marginal) could indicate an over-damped oscillatory recovery if the apparatus was perturbed. A mechanical shock or temperature change on day 11 might have set the pendulum into a slow recovery with undershoot, producing negative correlation at lag ~7–9 days. However, this predicts that readings should gradually return toward baseline by day 20+, which I cannot yet test. This is a sub-hypothesis of the mechanical perturbation scenario and is kept separate only because it makes a testable prediction about future readings (convergence back to baseline). Currently low probability because I have no strong evidence that the shift is temporary rather than permanent.

hypotheses.label: Measurement noise dominates; all cross-instrument correlations and auto-correlations are statistical flukes
hypotheses.rationale: Some correlations marginally exceed chance (e.g., resonator_obs ↔ resonator_obs at 0-day offset: 0.334 vs ±0.374), but many lie within chance bounds. With small n per cross-check (n=12–78) and multiple comparisons (6 cross-checks × ~20 lag offsets = ~120 correlations tested), false positives are expected by chance alone. Mundane candidates: (i) thermal transient in days 11–16 (pendulums respond faster, resonators lag by ~4 days as heat penetrates mechanical resonators); (ii) pressure or humidity shift in the settlement air (would lengthen pendulum periods and increase damping on resonators); (iii) a calibration drift or instrument adjustment performed on day 12 (pendulums) and day 16 (resonators) by different operators.
